summary: Describes how to encrypt LISP-encapsulated traffic, using existing LISP control-plane mechanisms for key exchange, to protect the data plane from third-party surveillance. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: This locks the messages in a sealed box while they travel between LISP sites, so strangers cannot read them.

questions: what is lisp data plane confidentiality
what are the lisp kk bits
which cipher suites does lisp crypto use
subtitle: Encrypting LISP-encapsulated traffic, with keys negotiated inside the existing Map-Request and Map-Reply exchange.

tldr.problem: LISP routers encapsulate packets that may travel in plaintext across the network between sites, open to third-party surveillance.
tldr.mechanism: An ITR and ETR run a Diffie-Hellman exchange inside the Map-Request and Map-Reply messages, derive symmetric keys, and the ITR encrypts the payload with an AEAD cipher. Two KK bits in the LISP header say which key was used.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol that gives LISP data-plane confidentiality without a separate PKI, with up to three keys per ETR for fast rekeying.

today: RFC 8061 is an Experimental specification, published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation, and it is not an Internet Standards Track document. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Goals and Requirements
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP, RFC 6830) lets routers map non-routable Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) to routable Routing Locators (RLOCs). Ingress Tunnel Routers (ITRs) and Proxy ITRs (PITRs) encapsulate packets toward Egress Tunnel Routers (ETRs) and Re-encapsulating Tunnel Routers (RTRs). The packets that reach the ITR may be unencrypted, so nothing protects the data on the path.

This document encrypts the user payload between the encapsulator and the decapsulator. If the source host already encrypts its traffic, LISP does not need to. The encryption is unidirectional: return traffic uses the same procedures with different key values.

The design requirements include: no separate Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), a key exchange budget of one round-trip time (a two-packet exchange), symmetric keying in the data plane, rekeying when keys are compromised, authenticated encryption with integrity checks, and support for multiple Cipher Suites.
sections.eli5: When a letter is handed to the delivery truck, anyone along the road could peek at it. This puts the letter in a locked box first, and it does so without needing a big new office to hand out keys.

sections.title: Key Exchange in Map-Request and Map-Reply
sections.content:
The RFC deliberately does not store security keys in the LISP mapping system. Instead, the ITR and ETR negotiate shared secrets in the Map-Request and Map-Reply messages they already exchange when the ITR needs the RLOC of an ETR.

The exchange is a Diffie-Hellman one. Both sides use the same parameters p and g. The ITR computes its public key I and sends it in the Map-Request. The ETR computes its own public key E, returns it in the Map-Reply, and can already compute the shared secret s. When the ITR receives the reply, it computes the same s.

The key material is carried in the LISP Security Key LCAF type (RFC 8060), with AFI 16387 and type 11. A Key Count field says how many keys are included, up to a maximum of three, identified as key-id 1, 2 and 3. The R bit SHOULD be sent as 0 and MUST be ignored on receipt.

If the ETR does not want encrypted traffic, it returns a Map-Reply with no Security Key LCAF in its RLOC-records, which tells the ITR not to encrypt. If the ITR offered several key-ids and the ETR wants only some, it replies only for those.
sections.eli5: Two friends each mix a secret color with a shared color and swap the mixtures. Each then adds their own secret again and both end up with the same new color, which nobody watching could work out.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Key Derivation
sections.content:
The 8-bit Cipher Suite field selects the Diffie-Hellman group and the cipher, integrity and key derivation function (KDF). Six suites are defined, and 0 is reserved. They cover 2048-bit and 3072-bit MODP groups and Curve25519, combined with AES-128 in CBC or GCM mode or with ChaCha20-Poly1305. All use HMAC-SHA-256 as the KDF.

Once the Diffie-Hellman shared secret exists, a counter-mode KDF per NIST SP 800-108 turns it into data-plane keys. The KDF key is the shared secret, and the context is a two-octet counter, the null-terminated string lisp-crypto, the ITR's nonce from the Map-Request, and the number of bits required, as a two-octet value. If more keying material is needed than one call returns, the counter is incremented and the KDF is called again.

The most significant 256 bits of the derived material are used as the AEAD key, which is split into a 128-bit encryption key and a 128-bit integrity check key inside the cipher.
sections.eli5: The secret the two sides agreed on is stirred together with a recipe to make the actual lock-and-key pair. Different recipes (cipher suites) are listed by number so both sides pick the same one.

sections.title: Data-Plane Operation
sections.content:
The LISP header gets two new KK bits, taken from previously unused flag bits. KK of 00 means the packet is not encrypted. A value of 1, 2 or 3 is the key-id of the key used. When KK is not zero, an Initialization Vector (IV) is placed before the payload, and its length depends on the Cipher Suite.

Because all defined suites are AEAD, no separate integrity check value field is needed; it is part of the ciphertext. The LISP header, the IV and the payload are covered as associated data. The outer IP header, UDP header and LISP header travel as plaintext, and the packet payload after the header is encrypted.

To encapsulate, the sender creates the IV, encrypts the payload with the AEAD key, prepends the LISP header with the right key-id, and then prepends the UDP and outer IP headers. For GCM suites the IV is incremented per packet starting at 1, and for CBC suites it is a new random number per packet.

To decapsulate, the receiver strips the headers, looks up the AEAD key by key-id in a local cache, and decrypts. If the integrity check fails, the packet is invalid and is discarded. Otherwise it is forwarded to the destination EID.
sections.eli5: The outside of the envelope (the address) stays readable so the mail can be delivered. Only the letter inside is locked, and a number on the envelope tells the receiver which key opens it.

sections.title: Dynamic Rekeying
sections.content:
Since up to three keys can be carried in both control and data messages, an ITR can keep encrypting with one key while it negotiates others with the same ETR. RLOC-probing can be used to change keys or Cipher Suites at any time.

A rekeying event happens when an ITR or PITR changes the Cipher Suite or public key in the Map-Request. The ETR compares what it last saw for that key-id, and if anything changed, it computes a new public key and returns it in the Map-Reply. The ITR must not use the corresponding key-id in packets until it receives a Map-Reply with the Cipher Suite value it expects.

If rekeying is not wanted during RLOC-probing, the ITR can leave out the Security Key LCAF or send the same key material it last received from the ETR.
sections.eli5: It is like changing the lock on a door while keeping a second key in use, so you never get locked out while the new lock is being set up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Area Advisory Group (SAAG) advised the working group: do not use asymmetric ciphers in the data plane, consider ECDH early, add Cipher Suites because ciphers are created more often than protocols, and use AEAD so authentication comes with encryption.

The key exchange runs over a public, non-secure network, so a man in the middle (MITM) acting as a Map-Replier could supply its own public key and share a secret with the ITR. If it also sits in the data path, it could decrypt the ITR's traffic. LISP can secure Map-Replies with the authentication process in LISP-SEC. When signature verification fails, the ITR discards the key exchange parameters, avoids using that ETR, and logs a severe message to the network administrator.
sections.eli5: The risk is a stranger pretending to be your friend while you swap the color mixtures. A signature on the reply works like a seal that proves the friend really sent it.
